title: Cleft lip & palate
scenario: Picture of a right unilateral complete cleft lip. Archive
Picture of a complete bilateral cleft lip (written station; similar, very clear picture). 430F
Picture of a complete LEFT cleft lip. 436F · 437A
Unmanned station — picture (left unilateral complete cleft lip). 439A

imgs.cap: Right unilateral complete cleft lip Left unilateral cleft lip (437A/439A, similar picture)
Complete bilateral cleft lip Bilateral cleft lip (infant)

qs.q: What is the abnormality seen in the picture? (describe it)
a: State side + complete/incomplete + uni/bilateral: e.g. "right unilateral complete cleft lip", "complete bilateral cleft lip".
qs.why: A complete diagnosis names side, extent and laterality — that's what examiners mark.

qs.q: What are the classifications of cleft lip and palate?
a: Unilateral or bilateral; complete or incomplete (partial); combined (lip + palate) or isolated.
qs.why: Clefts are described by side (uni/bilateral), extent (complete reaches the nostril floor) and which structures are involved (lip, palate or both).

qs.q: What is the Veau classification? Mention the classes.
a: I: soft palate only · II: soft + hard palate · III: complete unilateral cleft of lip, palate & alveolus · IV: complete bilateral cleft of lip, palate & alveolus.
qs.why: Veau grades palatal clefts by increasing extent: soft palate → hard palate → unilateral complete → bilateral complete.

qs.q: What are the possible complications? (of this patient / of cleft palate)
a: Feeding problems (poor suction, nasal regurgitation), speech problems, recurrent otitis media (Eustachian-tube dysfunction), recurrent chest infections/aspiration, dental
abnormalities/malocclusion, nasal deformity, cosmetic & psychosocial problems.
qs.why: The open palate breaks the oral–nasal seal (feeding, speech, aspiration), the palatal muscles can't open the Eustachian tube (otitis media), and the alveolar cleft disturbs teeth.

qs.q: What is the most common deformity associated with cleft lip?
a: Nasal deformity.
qs.why: The lip muscle pulls the alar base and nasal cartilages abnormally, so a nasal deformity accompanies every cleft lip.

qs.q: What is the most affected muscle?
a: Cleft lip: orbicularis oris (437A answer). Cleft palate: levator veli palatini.
qs.why: The orbicularis oris is divided in a cleft lip; the levator veli palatini is abnormally inserted in a cleft palate — both must be reconstructed.

qs.q: What are the important questions in the history? / Mention the risk factors.
a: Feeding problems, failure to gain weight, recurrent ear infections.
Pregnancy: anticonvulsants/medications, alcohol, smoking, maternal age; family history of clefts; syndromes (e.g. Down).
qs.why: Ask about feeding, weight gain and ears (complications), and the risk factors — family history, maternal smoking, medications (anticonvulsants), syndromes.
hist: Feeding problems, failure to gain weight
The open palate prevents suction, so feeding is difficult and weight gain is poor.
The abnormal palatal muscles can't open the Eustachian tube → otitis media with effusion.
Phenytoin and other teratogens cause clefts.
Clefts can be part of a syndrome (e.g. Pierre Robin, Down) that needs further assessment.

qs.q: What instructions/advice would you give the mother?
a: Feed upright (45°); use a squeezable bottle / special nipple (pigeon); burp frequently; lip taping/adhesion for the first months; refer to the cleft team.
qs.why: Upright feeding with special squeezable bottles overcomes the poor seal and reduces nasal regurgitation; early referral to the cleft team coordinates care.

qs.q: What is the treatment?
a: Multidisciplinary cleft team; surgical cleft-lip repair (cheiloplasty), later palate repair.
qs.why: Clefts need a multidisciplinary team; surgery repairs the lip first, then the palate, with speech, ENT and dental follow-up.

qs.q: When do you operate? / What is the timing of the repairs?
a: Lip: 3–6 months (usually ~3–4 months) — "rule of 10s": weight 10 lb, age 10 weeks, Hb 10 g/dL (WBC < 10 000).
Palate: 9–12 months (~1 year). Alveolar bone graft: 8–12 years (after canine eruption).
Rhinoplasty: 16 (girls) / 18 (boys).

Full timeline (437 file): counselling in utero–3 weeks · pre-surgical orthodontics 2–4 weeks · lip 3–6 months · palate ± ear tubes 9–14 months · speech assessment 3 months after the palate · VPI surgery 5–7 years · secondary nasal repair 5–6 years · alveolar bone graft 7–12 years · orthognathic surgery 16 (F) / 18 (M) · adult rhinoplasty > 18.
qs.why: Each repair is timed to development: lip at ~3 months (rule of 10s) for safe anaesthesia, palate by ~1 year before speech develops, alveolar bone graft before the canine erupts, rhinoplasty after facial growth.

qs.q: Why repair at 3–4 months?
a: Not earlier — anaesthetic risk; not later — psychological impact on the parents and child.
qs.why: Earlier carries higher anaesthetic risk in a small baby; later prolongs the psychosocial burden and feeding difficulty.

tips.t: Don't forget to write/say the location (side).

notes.t: The older files answered "levator veli palatini" — that is for the palate; for the lip it is orbicularis oris.

extra.q: Syndromes associated with cleft lip & palate
a: Down syndrome, Apert syndrome (also Pierre Robin, Van der Woude).

title: Hypertrophic scar & keloid
seen_note: 436A — listed only ("keloid scar"); 438A — same as previous files" (keloid scar)
scenario: A patient comes 2 months after a laceration of the abdomen sutured in the ER, with this scar. Archive Keloid picture (ear). 439B · Archive

imgs.cap: Raised scar confined to the wound — hypertrophic scar Keloid of the ear lobe

qs.q: Give the 2 most likely differential diagnoses.
a: Hypertrophic scar, keloid scar.
qs.why: An overgrown raised scar after a laceration is either hypertrophic or keloid.

qs.q: How can you differentiate them clinically?
a: Keloid extends beyond the borders of the original wound (doesn't regress); hypertrophic stays within the wound borders (may regress).
qs.why: Keloids grow beyond the wound margins and don't regress; hypertrophic scars stay within them and often improve.

qs.q: Mention 2 factors that may contribute to this condition.
a: Tension (tight suturing), infection, smoking (also wound site, delayed healing, dark skin).
qs.why: Tension, infection and delayed healing increase scar overgrowth.

qs.q: Mention 3 non-invasive treatments.
a: Pressure garments, silicone sheets/gel, intralesional steroid (triamcinolone) injection, laser.
qs.why: Pressure, silicone and intralesional steroids reduce collagen formation and flatten the scar.

qs.q: Mention 1 invasive treatment.
a: Surgical excision / scar revision.
qs.why: Excision/revision can remove the scar (with adjuvant steroids for keloids, which recur after excision alone).

qs.q: What is the diagnosis? (ear picture)
a: Keloid scar — overgrows the original wound edges.
qs.why: Scar tissue extending beyond the original wound (e.g. earlobe after piercing) = keloid.

qs.q: Define the pathology.
a: Fibroproliferative disorder: fibroblasts up-regulate collagen synthesis and deposition, driven by profibrotic cytokines (TGF-β1) and failure of apoptosis of activated fibroblasts.
qs.why: Keloids are a fibroproliferative disorder: overactive fibroblasts lay down excess collagen driven by TGF-β.

qs.q: Mention one risk factor.
a: Genetic predisposition — African (dark-skinned) populations (also age 10–30, sites: ear lobe, sternum, shoulders).
qs.why: Keloids are commoner in darker skin, young people and certain sites (earlobe, sternum, shoulders).

qs.q: Mention one treatment modality.
a: Mature keloids: monitor, or excise + adjuvant therapy — intralesional steroid, radiotherapy, cryotherapy, laser, pressure, antitumour/immunosuppressive agents.
qs.why: Keloids recur after excision alone, so excision is combined with steroids, radiotherapy or pressure.

title: Burns (thermal, inhalation & chemical)
scenario: Burn station — classification, TBSA and management. Archive
A patient with major burns and suspected inhalation injury (unmanned, 10 marks). 441F · 442B
Scald burn picture with eschar and leathery skin, no bone showing — chemical burn questions. Archive

imgs.cap: Deep (full-thickness) burn of the hand with leathery eschar

qs.q: What is your first management, and why?
a: Primary survey — airway first: look for inhalation injury (facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot around mouth/nose, hoarseness, stridor, carbonaceous sputum) → 100 % O₂ and early endotracheal intubation.
Why: airway oedema progresses rapidly and makes later intubation very difficult or impossible.
qs.why: Inhalation injury causes rapidly progressive airway oedema — secure the airway early before it closes.

qs.q: How do you calculate the TBSA?
a: Wallace rule of nines (adult): head & neck 9, each arm 9, anterior trunk 18, posterior trunk 18, each leg 18, perineum 1.
Palm of the patient (with fingers) ≈ 1 % — for scattered burns; Lund & Browder chart for children (child: head 18, each leg 14).
Count only partial- and full-thickness burns.
qs.why: TBSA drives fluid calculation and referral; rule of nines for adults, palm method for scattered burns, Lund–Browder for children (larger head).

qs.q: How do you resuscitate?
a: 2 large-bore IV cannulas (through unburned skin), urinary catheter (target UOP ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults, 1 mL/kg/h in children), monitor BP, HR, SpO₂, urine output.
qs.why: Burns cause massive fluid shifts — large-bore access and urine output monitoring guide resuscitation.

qs.q: How do you manage the fluids?
a: Parkland: 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA of Ringer's lactate in 24 h — half in the first 8 h from the time of burn, half over the next 16 h.
qs.why: Parkland estimates the fluid needed; half is given in the first 8 h from the time of the burn because losses peak early.

qs.q: The burn is circumferential — what is the management?
a: Escharotomy (look for pain, tense limb, ↓ capillary refill, weak/absent distal pulses, restricted chest movement); fasciotomy if compartment syndrome develops.
qs.why: Inelastic eschar around a limb or chest acts as a tourniquet — escharotomy releases it to restore circulation/ventilation.

qs.q: Classify the burn according to depth.
a: Superficial (epidermal, erythema — sunburn); superficial partial-thickness (blisters); deep partial-thickness (heals with scarring); full-thickness (needs skin graft).
qs.why: Depth decides healing: superficial and superficial partial heal from skin appendages; deep partial and full thickness need grafting.

qs.q: Classify the burn according to degree.
a: 1st: intact red skin · 2nd: red–white with blisters (mottled if deep) · 3rd: white, thick, leathery eschar, thrombosed vessels, painless · 4th: involves fat, muscle, bone.
qs.why: The degree classification describes the same depths by appearance and sensation (full thickness is painless — nerves destroyed).

qs.q: What degree of burn is this (picture)?
a: Third-degree (full-thickness) burn.
qs.why: White/leathery, painless skin with thrombosed vessels = full-thickness (third-degree) burn.

qs.q: Which injuries need referral to a burn centre (American Burn Association)?
a: Partial-thickness > 10 % TBSA; face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, major joints; any 3rd- degree; electrical (incl. lightning); chemical; inhalation injury; pre-existing illness; concomitant trauma; children in hospitals without paediatric facilities; special social/rehabilitation needs.
qs.why: The ABA criteria identify burns needing specialist care — large, deep, special areas, special mechanisms or complicated patients.

qs.q: What is the management of the burn?
a: General: ABC, IV fluids (Parkland), analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, antibiotics if needed, NGT, Foley, nutritional support.
Local: escharotomy, debridement, excision & skin grafting (deep partial/full thickness); superficial partial → dressings (fucidin / silver sulfadiazine), heal in ~2 weeks.
qs.why: Systemic care (fluids, analgesia, nutrition, tetanus) plus local care: dressings for superficial burns, early excision and grafting for deep ones.

qs.q: What are the types of chemical burns?
a: Alkali and acid.
qs.why: Chemical burns are from acids (coagulative necrosis) or alkalis (liquefactive necrosis — penetrate deeper, worse).

qs.q: What is the first aid for chemical burns?
a: Remove clothing and aggressively irrigate with water / normal saline for at least 30–60 min.
qs.why: Prolonged copious irrigation dilutes and removes the chemical; neutralising agents are avoided (heat release).

qs.q: Which specific burn can cause hypocalcaemia?
a: Hydrofluoric acid (treat with calcium gluconate gel/injection).
qs.why: Fluoride ions bind calcium — hydrofluoric acid causes hypocalcaemia, treated with calcium gluconate.

title: Basal cell carcinoma & skin cancer
scenario: Picture of a lesion on the face/nose of an old patient. Archive
A similar picture — benign vs malignant differentials. Archive

imgs.cap: Pearly nodular lesion with rolled edge and telangiectasia — basal cell carcinoma

qs.q: Describe what you see.
a: Pearly, nodular lesion with a rolled edge, surface telangiectasia, sharp smooth margin (± central ulceration).
qs.why: Describe the lesion's surface, edge and vessels — a pearly rolled edge with telangiectasia is the classic BCC description.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Basal cell carcinoma.
qs.why: A pearly nodule with telangiectasia on the face of an older patient = basal cell carcinoma.

qs.q: Mention 2 features that support your diagnosis.
a: Face / sun-exposed site, telangiectasia, rolled pearly edge/ulceration, old age.
qs.why: BCC arises in sun-exposed skin of older people; the rolled pearly edge and telangiectasia are its hallmarks.

qs.q: What else do you want to examine?
a: Rest of the facial skin & scalp, other sun-exposed areas, mouth & nose, cervical lymph nodes.
qs.why: Sun damage is field-wide — look for other skin cancers and the regional nodes.

qs.q: Mention 3 differential diagnoses.
a: Squamous cell carcinoma, malignant melanoma, naevus, seborrhoeic keratosis
(keratoacanthoma).
qs.why: The main skin-lesion differentials include the other skin cancers and common benign pigmented/keratotic lesions.

qs.q: Two non-malignant differential diagnoses?
a: Epidermal inclusion cyst, dermatofibroma (also seborrhoeic keratosis, naevus).
qs.why: Benign mimics include cysts, dermatofibroma, naevi and seborrhoeic keratosis.

qs.q: Two malignant differential diagnoses?
a: BCC, SCC, melanoma.
qs.why: The three malignant skin tumours to consider are BCC, SCC and melanoma.

qs.q: What is the rate of metastasis?
a: Rare.
qs.why: BCC invades locally but almost never metastasises.

qs.q: What is the growth rate?
a: Slow, steady and insidious.
qs.why: BCCs grow slowly over months to years ("rodent ulcer" erodes locally).

qs.q: How do you differentiate melanoma from a benign lesion?
a: ABCDE: Asymmetry, irregular Border, heterogeneous Colour, Diameter > 6 mm, Evolving.
qs.why: ABCDE criteria flag the features that distinguish melanoma from a benign naevus.

qs.q: How would you investigate this patient?
a: Biopsy to confirm — punch biopsy (or excisional biopsy).
qs.why: Histology confirms the diagnosis and subtype — punch or excisional biopsy.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Surgical excision with a safe margin (most common; Mohs for high-risk facial sites). Non-surgical: radiotherapy, imiquimod cream, photodynamic therapy, cryotherapy.
qs.why: Excision with clear margins cures most BCCs; Mohs surgery saves tissue on the face; non-surgical options suit superficial lesions or unfit patients.

qs.q: Squamous cell carcinoma — how do you diagnose/manage it?
a: Excisional biopsy (excision with 4–6 mm margin); assess regional nodes; radiotherapy if inoperable.
qs.why: SCC can metastasise to nodes, so it is excised with wider margins and the nodes are assessed.

title: Carpal tunnel syndrome
scenario: An elderly patient with muscle wasting, weakness and numbness in both hands (radial 3 fingers), worse on the right. 438F · 439F · 442A

imgs.cap: Bilateral thenar wasting (arrows) 442A exam picture — thenar wasting

qs.q: What do you see in the picture?
a: Thenar muscle wasting.
qs.why: Flattening of the thenar eminence = thenar wasting (median-supplied muscles).

qs.q: What is the diagnosis / differential diagnosis?
a: Carpal tunnel syndrome (DDx: cervical radiculopathy C6/7, peripheral neuropathy, motor neurone disease).
qs.why: Thenar wasting with radial 3½-digit numbness = carpal tunnel syndrome; cervical radiculopathy and neuropathy are the mimics.

qs.q: What muscles and nerve are affected?
a: Thenar muscles (APB, opponens pollicis) — median nerve.
qs.why: The recurrent motor branch of the median nerve supplies APB and opponens pollicis.

qs.q: Which fingers are affected?
a: Median-nerve distribution: thumb, index, middle and the radial half of the ring finger (3½).
qs.why: The median nerve supplies sensation to the radial 3½ digits.

qs.q: What special tests would you do?
a: Phalen's test and Tinel's test (+ carpal compression test).
qs.why: Phalen's (wrist flexion) and Tinel's (tapping) provoke symptoms by compressing/irritating the nerve.

qs.q: What is the definitive investigation?
a: Nerve conduction study (± EMG).
qs.why: Nerve conduction studies show slowed conduction across the wrist and grade severity.

qs.q: What is the conservative management?
a: Lifestyle/activity modification, night wrist splint, NSAIDs, steroid injection into the carpal tunnel.
qs.why: Splinting at night and activity change relieve pressure in mild disease; steroid injection reduces swelling.

qs.q: What is the surgical (definitive) treatment?
a: Carpal tunnel release (division of the transverse carpal ligament).
qs.why: Dividing the transverse carpal ligament decompresses the nerve — the definitive cure.

title: Wound healing — primary vs secondary closure (laceration)
seen_note: 438B — listed only ("wound primary and second intention")
scenario: Two pictures — identify primary and secondary closure. 435
Picture of a wound on the dorsum of the hand. 441A

qs.q: Picture 1 / Picture 2 — identify the type of closure.
a: Pic 1: primary closure (primary intention — edges approximated with sutures). Pic 2: secondary closure (secondary intention — wound left open, heals by granulation/contraction).
qs.why: Primary intention = edges brought together with sutures; secondary intention = the wound is left open to fill with granulation tissue and contract.

qs.q: What are the risk factors for failed healing?
a: Infection, old age, DM, smoking (also malnutrition, steroids, ischaemia, radiation).
qs.why: Infection, diabetes, smoking, age, malnutrition, steroids and ischaemia all impair healing.

qs.q: When should the patient ideally stop smoking?
a: At least 4 weeks before surgery.
qs.why: Smoking reduces tissue oxygen; stopping ≥ 4 weeks before surgery significantly reduces wound complications.

qs.q: Describe what you see. (hand wound)
a: Laceration on the dorsum of the hand — site, length, depth, edges, contamination/foreign bodies, exposed tendons.
qs.why: Describe the wound fully — site, size, depth, edges, contamination and exposed structures.

qs.q: How will you treat it in the ER?
a: Irrigation, remove debris/foreign bodies (debridement), then suture — primary closure (the examiner asked the type: primary).
qs.why: A clean, fresh laceration is irrigated, debrided and closed primarily.

qs.q: What else do you want to do?
a: Full neurovascular examination of the hand and test the extensor tendons (some examiners wanted detailed neuro, some asked the tendon names); tetanus prophylaxis.
qs.why: Dorsal hand wounds often cut extensor tendons and nerves — examine them all, and give tetanus prophylaxis.

title: Melanoma
scenario: Picture of a pigmented skin lesion. Archive

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Malignant melanoma.
qs.why: An irregular, variably pigmented lesion = malignant melanoma until histology says otherwise.

qs.q: Give 2 other differential diagnoses.
a: Pigmented basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma (also seborrhoeic keratosis, atypical naevus).
qs.why: Pigmented BCC, SCC, seborrhoeic keratosis and atypical naevi can mimic melanoma.

qs.q: Give 3 malignant features.
a: ABCDE: asymmetry, irregular borders, heterogeneous colour, diameter > 6 mm, evolving.
qs.why: ABCDE — asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variation, diameter > 6 mm and evolution — are the malignant features.

qs.q: What can you use to stage this lesion?
a: Excisional biopsy → Breslow thickness (+ ulceration, mitoses) → TNM (AJCC); sentinel lymph- node biopsy.
qs.why: Breslow thickness on excisional biopsy is the most important prognostic factor; sentinel node biopsy stages the nodes.

qs.q: What is the treatment?
a: Wide local excision (margins by Breslow thickness) ± sentinel node biopsy.
qs.why: Wide local excision with margins chosen by Breslow thickness, plus sentinel node biopsy for thicker lesions.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries
scenario: Written station — peripheral nerves. Old exam

qs.q: A patient lost shoulder abduction — which nerve is injured?
a: Axillary nerve.
qs.why: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid — injury loses shoulder abduction.

qs.q: A patient lost extension of the fingers — which nerve?
a: Posterior interosseous nerve.
qs.why: The posterior interosseous nerve supplies the finger extensors (wrist extension is kept by ECRL above it).

qs.q: A patient cannot make an "O" with the thumb and index finger — which nerve?
a: Anterior interosseous nerve.
qs.why: The AIN supplies FPL and index FDP — without them the thumb IP and index DIP can't flex to make an "O".

qs.q: A patient with Froment's sign — which nerve?
a: Ulnar nerve.
qs.why: Froment's sign shows weak adductor pollicis (ulnar) — FPL (median) flexes the thumb to compensate.

title: Erb's palsy
scenario: A 4.5 kg baby girl born after a traumatic normal delivery (written station; similar, very clear picture). 430A

imgs.cap: "Waiter's tip" posture of the left arm — Erb's palsy

qs.q: What is the abnormality seen in the picture?
a: Erb's (Erb–Duchenne) palsy.
qs.why: An adducted, internally rotated arm with pronated forearm after a difficult delivery = Erb's palsy.

qs.q: Which side is affected?
a: The left upper limb.
qs.why: State the affected side from the picture.

qs.q: What nerve roots are involved?
qs.why: Erb's palsy is an upper-trunk injury (C5–C6 ± C7) from traction separating the head and shoulder.

qs.q: What is this posture called?
a: Waiter's tip posture.
qs.why: Loss of shoulder abductors/external rotators and elbow flexors/supinators leaves the arm adducted, internally rotated and pronated — the "waiter's tip".

qs.q: What dermatomes are supplied by the affected roots?
a: C5: tip of the shoulder & lateral arm · C6: lateral forearm, thumb & index · C7: middle finger.
qs.why: The C5–C7 dermatomes run along the lateral arm, lateral forearm, thumb/index and middle finger.
